chunks.title: Orbital disease: the framework
chunks.tldr: Signs: proptosis/dystopia, restricted motility, resistance to retropulsion. Think in 6 boxes: inflammatory (TED, IOIS, sarcoid, GPA, IgG4), infectious, neoplastic, trauma, malformation, vascular. History of cancer + new orbital mass = metastasis until proven otherwise. Hertel: normal ~17 mm, upper ~22–24; >2 mm asymmetry abnormal.
points: Pseudoproptosis: big myopic eye, fellow enophthalmos, lid retraction/contralateral ptosis, shallow orbits.
Exam: vitals/temp, VA, pupils, fields, colour, IOP (pulsatile mires?), motility, forced ductions, ant's-eye view, palpate rim, evert lids, V/VII function, nodes, fundus (folds, disc).
Imaging: CT or MRI with gadolinium + fat suppression; B-scan/Doppler for cystic/vascular.
Bloods as needed: TFTs/TSI/TPO, ACE, ANCA, LDH, IgG4, ANA, SPEP, FBC, U&E, HbA1c, cultures.
Biopsy as indicated (FNA limited role).
chunks.hook: Orbit boxes: 'I I N T M V' — Inflammatory, Infectious, Neoplastic, Trauma, Malformation, Vascular.

cards.a: More than 2 mm between the eyes.

cards.q: Patient with prior breast cancer and new orbital mass – presume?

chunks.title: Thyroid eye disease: signs
chunks.tldr: Upper lid retraction with lateral flare (most specific), lid lag (von Graefe), proptosis, restricted elevation > abduction (IR then MR fat). CT: muscle bellies thick, tendons spared; apical crowding. Compressive optic neuropathy in 5–7% — check every visit (RAPD, colour, fields, disc), often without much proptosis. ~80% hyperthyroid; eye course doesn't track thyroid control.
points: Muscle order: Inferior, Medial, Superior, Lateral ('I'M SLow'); isolated lateral rectus = not TED → work up.
IOP rises on upgaze (tight IR).
Euthyroid TED → TFTs every 6–12 months.
Ptosis or adduction deficit in thyroid patient → think myasthenia.
Lid retraction mimics: surgery, contralateral ptosis (Hering), aberrant III, Parinaud.
Myogenic (tight muscles, little proptosis) vs lipogenic (fat, big proptosis) variants.

cards.q: Most commonly enlarged extraocular muscle in TED?
Why can TED optic neuropathy occur without much proptosis?
cards.a: Tight enlarged muscles crowd the orbital apex while the globe can't decompress forward.

chunks.title: Thyroid eye disease: treatment
chunks.tldr: Stop smoking (document it every visit), endocrine referral, lubricate/tape/goggles, check vitamin D; selenium 100 µg b.i.d. × 6 months for mild active (women). Active moderate–severe: IV methylpred 500 mg weekly × 6 then 250 mg × 6, teprotumumab (IGF-1R), ± orbital radiotherapy (20 Gy). Optic neuropathy: oral/IV steroids → posterior (medial/lateral) decompression. Surgery order: decompression → squint → lids.
points: Decompression indications: optic neuropathy, severe exposure, globe luxation, uncontrollable IOP, disfiguring proptosis.
Steroids: DEXA, calcium/vit D, PPI, glucose monitoring; avoid chronic use.
Radiation: caution in diabetics (retinopathy) and vasculopaths.
Biologics (rituximab etc.) evidence mixed.
Review 3–6 monthly if mild; urgent if optic neuropathy or severe exposure.

cards.q: Correct sequence of surgery in TED?
cards.a: Orbital decompression, then strabismus surgery, then eyelid surgery.

chunks.title: Idiopathic orbital inflammation & IgG4
chunks.tldr: Explosive painful unilateral proptosis/motility loss (only 65% painful), boggy pink lids. Forms: myositis (tendon may be involved), dacryoadenitis, scleritis/tenonitis (ring sign), diffuse. Kids: bilateral in ⅓, fever/vomiting. Bilateral adults → search systemic cause. Rx: prednisone 1–1.2 mg/kg → dramatic response; no response → biopsy; radiation, methotrexate, biologics for recurrent. Biopsy lacrimal gland first if easy.
points: DDx: cellulitis, TED, sarcoid, GPA, IgG4, lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, mets (breast), leaking dermoid, lymphangioma bleed, CCF, necrotic melanoma.
Bone erosion → not IOIS.
Enhancement 'spills over' into adjacent fat on MRI.
Taper slowly; recurrences common.
IgG4-related: less explosive, enlarged infraorbital/sensory nerves, high IgG4 plasma cells on biopsy; ? lymphoma risk.
chunks.hook: Melts with steroids in a day or two = IOIS. Doesn't = biopsy.

cards.q: Imaging hint of IgG4-related orbital disease?
cards.a: Enlargement of sensory nerves (e.g., infraorbital nerve).

cards.q: What if IOIS doesn't respond dramatically to steroids?
cards.a: Biopsy to exclude lymphoma, metastasis or other causes.

chunks.title: Orbital cellulitis
chunks.tldr: Lid swelling + chemosis, proptosis, painful restricted motility, ± RAPD; usually from ethmoid sinusitis (also dental, trauma/FB, surgery, dacryocystitis). Admit, CT with contrast, cultures, ENT/ID. IV ampicillin-sulbactam or piperacillin-tazobactam (+ vancomycin if MRSA/meningitis), 48–72 h then oral to complete 10–14 days. Diabetic/immunocompromised → mucormycosis (black eschar, acidosis).
points: Kids: H. influenzae rare if vaccinated; trauma → gram-negatives; dental → aggressive anaerobes.
Penicillin-allergic: vanco + ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or FQ + metronidazole.
Decongestant spray ≤3 days; canthotomy if tight orbit/optic neuropathy.
Steroids after 24–48 h of IV antibiotics may shorten stay (kids).
Review twice daily; worse after 48–72 h → repeat CT (abscess?).
Non-improvers: abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, MRSA, dental source, non-infectious cause, non-compliance.
chunks.hook: Sinus + proptosis + sore eye movements = orbital cellulitis → admit, IV, CT.

cards.q: Orbital infection to fear in a diabetic with ketoacidosis?

chunks.title: Subperiosteal abscess & cavernous sinus thrombosis
chunks.tldr: Suspect SPA if cellulitis fails or worsens after 48–72 h of IV antibiotics → repeat contrast CT. Age rule (Harris): <9 yrs sterile/single aerobe, 93% settle on antibiotics; 9–14 mixed; >14 mixed with anaerobes → drain. Drain urgently if optic neuropathy, large (>1250 mm³ in kids), frontal sinus. Cavernous sinus thrombosis: septic, multiple palsies, bilateral → ICU, antibiotics, drain source, ± anticoagulation.
points: Drain sinuses with the abscess (fewer recurrences); leave orbital drain 24–48 h.
Imaging lags clinical improvement 48–72 h — don't rescan unless worse.
Intraorbital (intraconal) abscess rare: trauma, FB, surgery.
chunks.hook: Little kids' abscesses melt; teenagers' need a knife.

cards.q: When should a subperiosteal abscess be drained urgently?
cards.a: Optic neuropathy, large abscess, frontal sinus involvement, age >14/anaerobes, or failure to improve.

chunks.title: Acute dacryoadenitis
chunks.tldr: Pain/swelling of outer third of upper lid, S-shaped lid, red palpebral lobe, temporal chemosis. Usually inflammatory (IOIS); viral (mumps, EBV — bilateral), bacterial rare (Staph, gonococcus). Bacterial/unclear → antibiotics; inflammatory → steroids. Biopsy if atypical/persistent (lymphoma, sarcoid, IgG4, malignant tumour).
points: DDx: hordeolum, preseptal/orbital cellulitis, leaking dermoid, rhabdomyosarcoma (kids), lacrimal malignancy (pain from perineural spread), retained FB.

cards.q: Classic lid sign of lacrimal gland enlargement?

chunks.title: Orbital tumours in children
chunks.tldr: First rule out orbital cellulitis (commonest cause of proptosis in kids). Dermoid (superotemporal brow lump; excise intact). Infantile haemangioma (grows 6–9 months then involutes; worse with crying; propranolol if amblyopia risk). Rhabdomyosarcoma (~8–10 yrs, rapid proptosis → urgent biopsy; chemo + RT, good prognosis). Neuroblastoma mets (<5, periorbital ecchymosis, sick). Lymphangioma (bleeds after URTI, 'chocolate cyst', sclerotherapy). Optic glioma (2–6, NF1). Plexiform neurofibroma (S-lid, NF1). Leukaemia (chloroma). LCH (lytic superotemporal lesion).
points: Propranolol: hypoglycaemia, bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm → paediatric monitoring.
Neuroblastoma can present as Horner in a child.
Hand–Schüller–Christian: exophthalmos + lytic bone + diabetes insipidus.
Granulocytic sarcoma may precede leukaemia by months.
Lymphangioma = 'crabgrass of the orbit' on imaging.
chunks.hook: Fast-growing orbital mass in a child = rhabdomyosarcoma until biopsy says otherwise.

cards.q: First-line treatment for vision-threatening infantile haemangioma?
Child with bilateral periorbital ecchymosis and proptosis?

chunks.title: Orbital tumours in adults
chunks.tldr: Cavernous venous malformation (commonest benign; middle-aged women, intraconal, encapsulated; grows in pregnancy). Solitary fibrous tumour (STAT6). Schwannoma, neurofibroma. ONSM (women, slow loss, optociliary shunts, tram-track; stereotactic RT). Mucocele (superonasal, frontal/ethmoid; endoscopic drainage). Lymphoma (salmon patch, superior/lacrimal, moulds to globe; RT ~24 Gy). Mets: breast (women, may cause enophthalmos), lung (men), prostate (bone).
points: Optic nerve sarcoid = 2nd commonest optic nerve lesion; MOGA mimics progressive NAION.
Lymphoma: biopsy fixed + fresh tissue; staging incl. bone marrow; lymphoid hyperplasia may become lymphoma.
NHL also melts with steroids — don't let response fool you.
Uveal mets 10× more common than orbital.
Well-circumscribed and symptomatic → excise; else observe 6–12 monthly.
chunks.hook: Scirrhous breast cancer pulls the eye IN (enophthalmos).

chunks.title: Lacrimal gland masses
chunks.tldr: Pleomorphic adenoma: slow painless, smooth fossa remodelling → excise whole, never incisional biopsy (recurrence/malignancy). Adenoid cystic carcinoma: pain (perineural), bone erosion, months → biopsy, excision + RT (± intra-arterial chemo); poor prognosis. Lymphoma: moulds to globe, salmon patch. Sarcoid (bilateral, ACE), IOIS, IgG4, dacryops, dermoid (excise intact).
points: Epithelial tumours unilateral; inflammation can be bilateral.
Temple/forehead pain = ominous.
Workup: CT orbit, chest CT, ACE, LDH, ANCA, IgG4, SPEP as needed.
Avoid steroids before biopsy.
Malignant mixed tumour: elderly, rapid, may arise in old pleomorphic adenoma.
chunks.hook: Painless + smooth = take it all out. Painful + bone eaten = cancer.

cards.q: Why not perform incisional biopsy on a suspected pleomorphic adenoma?
cards.a: Capsule breach causes recurrence and risk of malignant transformation; excise intact.

cards.q: Hallmark symptom of adenoid cystic carcinoma of the lacrimal gland?

chunks.title: Carotid–cavernous fistula & other
chunks.tldr: Direct CCF (young, trauma, high flow) vs indirect/dural (older, spontaneous). Signs: corkscrew arterialised vessels, chemosis, pulsatile proptosis, bruit, high IOP, venous congestion; mimics conjunctivitis/TED. CT: big superior ophthalmic vein; Doppler: reversed flow; angiography confirms (cortical venous drainage → stroke risk) → endovascular closure. Also intracranial meningioma extension, varix (proptosis with Valsalva).
points: Often misdiagnosed early as conjunctivitis or asymmetric glaucoma.
chunks.hook: Red eye that won't settle + corkscrew vessels + pulse in the eye = CCF.

cards.a: Enlarged superior ophthalmic vein (± enlarged muscles).
